chapters.title: Chapter 2: Trend, Support and Resistance on Currency Pairs

lessons.title: Trendlines, Channels and Moving Averages as Dynamic Support and Resistance

children.text: Deepak keeps redrawing his USD/INR trendline. Every few days, a candle pokes through it by a few paise right around the 9:00 am NSE open, so he erases the line and draws a new, shallower one connecting the lows including that spike. Within a week his "trendline" has been redrawn five times and tells him nothing useful. He has fallen into a trap you already have the tools to avoid, because you met this exact spike in Chapter 1.

body.text: Draw forex trendlines from candle body closes, not wick extremes, since session-open liquidity grabs create wicks that are not genuine price levels. And trust moving averages on major pairs a little more than you might on an individual stock, because enormous trend-following fund flows genuinely trade off them.

children.text: Trendlines: Draw From Bodies, Not Wicks

markDefs.definition: A line connecting a series of rising swing lows, in an uptrend, or falling swing highs, in a downtrend, used as a dynamic level that shifts with each new swing.

children.text: on a stock chart is usually drawn connecting swing lows or highs with reasonable confidence that each point reflects real trading. On forex, Chapter 1 already showed you that the first candle after a session open can carry a wick manufactured by resting orders clearing out, not genuine price discovery. If you anchor a trendline to one of those wicks, you are building your entire trend read on an artifact.

body.title: Illustrative USD/INR: A Trendline Anchored to a Body Survives a Session-Open Wick

children.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote. Day 3's low wick at 94.58 briefly pierces below the rising line of body closes and lows from Day 1 and Day 2. A trendline drawn to that wick would look broken. A trendline drawn to the candle bodies, using the close of 94.82, shows the uptrend fully intact, and Day 4 confirms it by pushing higher again. The wick was noise from the open, exactly as you saw in the previous chapter.

body.title: The trendline that would not stay drawn
body.scenario: Deepak's USD/INR trendline connects the candle lows, wicks included, over the past two weeks. Almost every session-open candle punches slightly below it, forcing him to redraw a shallower line each time, and his trendline has become nearly flat and useless for judging the trend.
body.prompt: What should Deepak change about how he draws the trendline, and why will that fix the constant redrawing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Deepak is anchoring his trendline to wick lows, which regularly include session-open liquidity grabs rather than genuine support.
2. He should redraw the trendline using candle body closes and lows, ignoring the wick extremes caused by thin liquidity right at the open.
3. A body-based trendline will not be broken by ordinary session-open noise, since that noise mostly shows up in the wick, not the close.
4. He should still respect a break that happens on a candle body close beyond the line, since that reflects a genuine shift, not just an opening spike.

children.text: Channels: Trading Between Two Parallel Lines

A channel is simply a trendline plus a second, parallel line drawn through the opposite swing points, the highs in an uptrend or the lows in a downtrend. Major forex pairs tend to respect channels for longer stretches than many individual stocks, because a currency's trend is usually driven by a small number of persistent macro forces, interest rate differentials, central bank stances and capital flows, rather than the constant stream of company-specific news that can knock a stock out of its channel.

body.title: Illustrative EUR/USD Rising Inside a Channel Over Eight Weeks
Where inside the channel would you look to buy?
body.question: EUR/USD is trending up inside a well-respected channel, as in the chart above. Weeks 3 and 6 both show pullbacks toward the lower boundary before price resumes climbing. Where within the channel does buying on a pullback offer the best risk-to-reward?
options: Near the upper boundary, right after a fresh high
Near the lower boundary, where the channel's rising trendline sits
Exactly in the middle of the channel
It does not matter, channels do not affect entry timing
body.explanation: Buying near the lower boundary, where the rising trendline provides support, gives you a close, logical stop just below the line and the full width of the channel as potential upside, the classic risk-to-reward edge of trading inside a respected channel.

children.text: Moving Averages as Dynamic Support and Resistance

A moving average smooths out day-to-day noise into a single line that moves with the trend, and pullbacks to it often act like support in an uptrend or resistance in a downtrend. This works on stocks too, but it tends to work unusually well on major currency pairs, because large systematic trend-following funds, often called CTAs, explicitly build strategies around widely watched averages such as the 50-day, 100-day and 200-day. When price approaches one of these lines, some of that buying or selling is not guesswork, it is programmed.

body.title: How a simple moving average is calculated

children.text: A simple moving average, or SMA, over a chosen number of periods is just the average of the closing prices over that window. As each new period closes, the oldest one drops off and the newest one is added.

content.caption: Simple moving average over n periods

body.title: Calculate the 5-day SMA
body.prompt: Using the five closes above, ₹95.10, ₹95.30, ₹95.20, ₹95.50 and ₹95.40, what is the 5-day simple moving average, in rupees?
body.explanation: The five closes add up to ₹476.50. Dividing by 5 gives a 5-day SMA of ₹95.30. As Day 6 closes, Day 1's ₹95.10 would drop out of the calculation and Day 6's close would be added in.

body.title: Illustrative USD/INR: Price Pulling Back to the 200-Day Moving Average Twice

body.text: Look at Weeks 4 and 7 above. Price dips down toward the 200-day moving average and bounces both times, a clean example of a moving average acting as dynamic support. This is illustrative, but the underlying reason it happens on real major pairs is not guesswork, it reflects systematic trend-following funds that genuinely add to positions around these widely watched averages.

children.text: Moving Averages on the Rupee: A Managed Float Wrinkle

USD/INR is not a free float like EUR/USD. RBI actively smooths sharp moves in the rupee, which tends to make USD/INR trends look unusually orderly on a moving average, fewer violent whipsaws than you might see on a stock. The flip side is that RBI's own comfort with certain round levels, the same psychological levels from Chapter 2's first lesson, can cap a moving-average breakout well before it runs as far as a similar setup might on a freely floating pair. A separate advanced-level course on central bank intervention covers RBI's footprint in full. For now, simply treat a moving-average breakout on USD/INR as a genuine signal, but size your expectations for how far it runs a little more conservatively than you would on EUR/USD.

body.title: Trendlines, Channels and Moving Averages: Key Terms

cards.definition: A line connecting rising swing lows or falling swing highs, best drawn from candle body closes on forex to avoid session-open wick noise.
A trendline plus a parallel line through the opposite swing points, forming a band the price tends to move within.
The average of closing prices over a set number of periods, used as a smoothed, dynamic support or resistance line.
A commodity trading advisor, a fund that runs systematic, rules-based strategies, often including trades that trigger around widely watched moving averages.
An exchange rate regime, like the rupee's, where the central bank actively smooths sharp moves rather than leaving the rate to trade completely freely.

points: Draw forex trendlines from candle body closes rather than wick extremes, since session-open liquidity grabs regularly produce wicks that are not genuine price levels.

Major currency pairs tend to respect channels for longer stretches than many stocks, since a currency's trend is usually driven by a few persistent macro forces rather than constant company-specific news.
Buying or selling near a channel's boundary, where the trendline itself provides a logical stop, offers a better risk-to-reward than acting in the middle of the channel.

Moving averages, especially the 50-day, 100-day and 200-day, tend to work unusually well as dynamic support and resistance on major pairs because systematic trend-following funds genuinely trade around them.
USD/INR's managed float makes its trends look smoother on a moving average than a freely floating pair, but RBI's comfort with round levels can also cap how far a moving-average breakout runs.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not trading advice. All chart examples are illustrative and not live or historical quotes. Trendlines, channels and moving averages are probabilistic tools that can and do fail, and should be combined with proper risk management before any trade.
